say.en: A baker starts alone, takes in two partners to open a second shop, later forms a private company to raise money from relatives, and one day lists it on the stock exchange. Each step changes who owns it and who bears the risk. In this lesson: State the meaning and features of the four business entities.
Distinguish them on members, liability, legal status and transfer of interest.
Choose a suitable form for a given business.

body.en: A *sole proprietorship* is owned, managed and controlled by one person, who takes all the profit and bears unlimited liability. It is easy to form and close, and decisions are quick, but capital and skills are limited and the business has no separate legal existence. A partnership is a relationship between persons who agree to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932). It has 2 to 50 partners (under the Companies Rules), more capital and skills, but partners have unlimited and joint liability, and interest cannot be transferred without the consent of all.

points.en: Sole proprietor: one owner, unlimited liability, no separate entity

title.en: On the board: Four entities compared

say.en: Compare the four forms on four points.
On the board: Four entities compared.

body.en: A company is an artificial person created by law (Companies Act, 2013), with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession, a common seal and limited liability of members. A *private* company has at least 2 and at most 200 members (excluding employees), restricts the transfer of its shares and cannot invite the public to buy its securities. A public company has at least 7 members with no maximum, its shares are freely transferable, and it can raise money from the public, which is why it is more strictly regulated. A one person company is a special private company with a single member.

points.en: Company: separate legal entity, limited liability, perpetual succession
*Private*: 2 to 200 members, shares not freely transferable, no public issue
*Public*: at least 7 members, free transfer, can invite the public

problem.en: Three friends want to start a software firm. They have ₹30 lakh, expect to need ₹2 crore within three years, and do not want to lose their homes if it fails. Which form suits them, and why?

steps.en: A partnership would give unlimited liability: their homes would be at risk.
A public company needs at least 7 members and heavy compliance: too much for now.
A private company gives limited liability, a separate legal entity and lets them bring in up to 200 investors privately.
Later, if they need large public funds, they can convert into a public company.

answer.en: A private limited company: limited liability now, with room to raise more capital later.
